title: Basic Chart Types
subtopics: Pie and doughnut charts: use cases and limitations
learning_outcomes: Explain basic chart types and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of basic chart types to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study basic chart types in the context of data visualization and storytelling. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Basic Chart Types matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: A visualization encodes values using position, length, area, color, and other channels. The chart type, axis, units, ordering, and annotations affect how readers interpret evidence.

items.title: Bar charts
items.text: Define bar charts in relation to basic chart types; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Line charts
items.text: Work through line charts using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Histograms
items.text: Check the edge cases for histograms: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Scatterplots
items.text: Document the rule or choice for scatterplots so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Pie and doughnut charts: use cases and limitations
items.text: Define pie and doughnut charts: use cases and limitations in relation to basic chart types; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by basic chart types. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Small multiples and structured panels help compare groups without overcrowding one chart.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: A visualization encodes values using position, length, area, color, and other channels. The chart type, axis, units, ordering, and annotations affect how readers interpret evidence. Next, connect this lesson to the linked prerequisite or following lesson. Record the method, input assumptions, observed result, and one limitation so another person can reproduce and review the work.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small synthetic example for basic chart types. State a question, make a prediction, trace or run an appropriate calculation, then write one finding and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
For SQL, use a local schema and read-only test data; this page does not provide a live database.
For package-dependent work, create an isolated environment and use the relevant official documentation.
